This produced a total of 34 sites across a fire interval chronosequence from 1 to 35years (or more), with each site containing one to five study species. The number of sites surveyed for each species ranged from 11 to 17, all spanning a similar post-fire chronosequence (Table [1\)](#page-3-0). Some sites were surveyed over two successive years, creating two nonindependent TSF samples. Sites were mostly (91%) located on Spearwood sands across a 100 km north–south extent of the Swan Coastal Plain (Figure [1](#page-4-0)). Mean annual rainfall ranged from 698 mm in the north (Muchea, 1971–2000) to 843 mm in the south (Halls Head, 1971–2000; Australian Bureau of Meteorology [2020](#page-17-10)) (Figure [S1\)](#page-20-8). All species except *B. prionotes* were sampled across the full extent of this rainfall gradient. *Banksia prionotes* was only found across a very narrow (negligible) range (30 mm mean annual rainfall difference) in the sampled study area, but occur more broadly in the region, as do the other study species. The presence (*n* = 19) or absence (*n* = 15) of kangaroos (western grey kangaroo, *Macropus fuliginosus*) as major herbivores was assessed at each site based on sightings of individuals or their scats as well as local knowledge and records (City of Joondalup [2015](#page-17-11); City of Nedlands [2014;](#page-17-12) Ecoscape (Australia Pty Ltd) [2008;](#page-18-22) Government of Western Australia [2000;](#page-19-21) Natural Area Consulting [2012](#page-19-22)). Where present in urban reserves, kangaroos (or signs of their presence) are easily observed, and populations often achieve high density. There was no discernible change in kangaroo abundance over the study period. #### **2.4   |   Field Surveys** At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [\(2024](#page-19-23)). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites. Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m2 as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m−2), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m−2). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plotbased surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table [1\)](#page-3-0). Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). These measurements were chosen to best represent how size relates to reproductive performance given each species' growth form. **FIGURE 1**    |    Locations of the 34 study sites in urban and peri-urban nature reserves on the Swan Coastal Plain around Perth, Western Australia. Some reserves contained multiple sites of various fire ages (some points obscured by other points). Mean annual rainfall follows a north–south (low-high) gradient indicated by the colour (light bluedark blue) of site location points (circles). Green shading indicates extant native vegetation, grey shading indicates urban areas and the solid red line indicates the boundary of the Swan Coastal Plain region (also shown on inset map). {5} === PAGE 7 === For trees with multiple stems, effective DBH (diameter of the summed cross-sectional area of all live stems) was calculated to produce a single representative value (Prior et al. [2011](#page-19-24)). Canopy volume (*V*, m3 ) for *H. hypericoides* and *A. humilis* was calculated from maximum canopy height (*H*, m) and perpendicular canopy width measurements (*W1* and *W2*, m), using an ellipsoid form: #### **2.5   |   Data Analysis** ## **2.5.1   |   Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories** To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert [2011](#page-17-13); Hurvich and Tsai [1989\)](#page-19-25). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli ([2011\)](#page-20-11). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson [2002\)](#page-17-14). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team [2020\)](#page-19-26) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. [2018\)](#page-18-23) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood [2017\)](#page-20-12). Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was logtransformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720mm) and 'high' (~790mm) rainfall sites, respectively. Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2m tall) on tree species that are typically >4m tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1year. Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4years) (Figure [S2\)](#page-20-8). #### **2.5.2**|**Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction** To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*2 ) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF. GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only. #### **3   |   Results** ## **3.1   |   Flowering Rates and Juvenile Periods** TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of flowering rates for all species (Table [2](#page-6-0)). While herbivory was found to impact the flowering rate of *H. hypericoides*, post-fire recovery was so rapid as to not alter the predicted juvenile period (Table [4\)](#page-8-0). High mean annual rainfall increased the juvenile period of *B. attenuata* by 5.7years (Table [4](#page-8-0)). ## **3.2   |   Flower and Cone Counts** TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of mean flower count and mean cone count per plant for all species (Table [5\)](#page-8-2). ### **4   |   Discussion**

## **4.1   |   Juvenile Periods and Tolerable Fire Intervals**

The shape of post-fire reproductive trajectories provides direct evidence of fire frequencies that permit species persistence and is critical information for the conservation and management of fire-prone ecosystems globally, especially with ongoing climate and fire regime change. We modelled reproduction in six woody plant species with a variety of fire-related traits across a range of fire ages in Banksia woodlands and found juvenile periods of 1–4 years, with little difference attributable to fire response type. Minimum tolerable fire intervals under average growing conditions based on primary juvenile periods for fire-killed species and a mix of primary and secondary juvenile periods for resprouters ranged from approximately 3–8 years and 2–9 years, respectively. Although there was some evidence of decline in reproduction in the oldest sites (>30 years since the last fire), reproductive capacity was likely still adequate for post-fire seedling recruitment after these long fire intervals. Variation in juvenile periods and reproductive output across all fire ages were associated with variation in growth forms and with changes in site productivity (rainfall) and herbivory. Taken together, our observations of rapid post-fire reproductive recovery and no fatal decline in reproduction in the long absence of fire are consistent with the suggestion that Banksia woodlands are adapted to mixed-severity fire regimes including widely varying intervals, where species have the capacity to cope with short and long fire intervals (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024\).

The species studied here, potentially representing a larger suite of Banksia woodland species with similar growth forms, fire response and seed bank storage modes, would all likely tolerate fire intervals of 10 years under average growing conditions, and the most rapidly maturing would likely tolerate intervals as short as 5 years under average growing conditions. While juvenile period data for resprouters is important for understanding effects on reproduction from seed, which is crucial for longterm population persistence, minimum tolerable fire intervals for resprouters based on the juvenile period method disregard the often-overriding contribution of resprouting to the post-fire recovery of species with this capability. Resprouters, therefore, may be able to tolerate even shorter intervals (i.e., less than 5 years) if resprouting capacity develops rapidly post-fire. However, several repeated short fire intervals (less than 5years) may preclude recruitment and erode adult resprouting capacity


{13}

=== PAGE 15 ===


(Enright et al. 2011; Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett 2016\), acting as a separate mechanism of sensitivity to short fire intervals (i.e., separate to immaturity risk). Rather than resprouters, a more appropriate focus for understanding community-level minimum tolerable fire intervals is the slowest maturing, firekilled species (*B. prionotes*). *Banksia prionotes* likely requires longer intervals of at least 8–10 years for sufficient post-fire recruitment where it occurs, especially where low rainfall delays or reduces flowering and seed production. Current managed fire interval objectives of 13–33 years for risk reduction (Ritchie et al. 2021\) should, therefore, support the persistence of the woody plant functional types studied here; however, continued regional warming and drying associated with climate change

may pose a threat of shortening wildfire intervals, consistent with the interval squeeze concept *sensu* (Enright et al. 2015).

Our juvenile period and minimum tolerable fire interval findings are consistent with evidence from the region on the same or similar species (Enright et al. 2014; Wilson et al. 2014\). However, corresponding minimum fire interval recommendations (8–16 years) suggested by Wilson et al. [\(2014) are based on population-level maturity of resprouters (a combination of primary and secondary juvenile periods) which, as explained above, are not the primary focus of the juvenile period approach as they largely recover via resprouting. Instead, minimum fire intervals based on juvenile period data for fire-killed species


{14}

=== PAGE 16 ===


presented in Wilson et al. [\(2014) are up to 8–10 years for the most sensitive, slow-maturing species, which is consistent with our findings.

Suggested minimum tolerable fire intervals for fire-killed serotinous species (including *B. prionotes*) in drier (less productive) shrublands north of our study region range from 10 to 15 years for high versus low post-fire winter rainfall years, respectively (Enright et al. 2014). As our minimum tolerable interval estimates (2–9 years) suggest, minimum tolerable fire intervals should be somewhat shorter in the more productive (higher rainfall) Banksia woodlands. Consistent with this hypothesis, our estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals of around 3–5 years for fire-killed shrubs with soil seed banks are somewhat shorter than the equivalent 5–6 years reported in Enright et al. [\(2014\). Interestingly, however, estimates for resprouting shrubs show little difference between the two regions; resprouting shrubs with canopy seed banks showed minimum tolerable intervals of around 5–7 years and resprouting shrubs with soil seed banks showed little risk of even the shortest intervals sampled (Enright et al. 2014). Post-fire growth and maturation rates of fire-killed shrubs, which regenerate from seedlings, are strongly contingent on environmental productivity (Gosper et al. 2022\), whereas post-fire growth rates in resprouting shrubs may be less contingent on environmental conditions during the post-fire period as already-established plants draw on stored energy reserves for post-fire growth and reproduction (Clarke et al. 2013), acknowledging again that seedling recruitment is not the major form of post-fire recovery for resprouters. A strength of the analysis of Enright et al. [\(2014\) is that estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals were based on robust, direct measures of resprouter survival and seedling recruitment, and therefore we suggest that further targeted study of seed availability and subsequent postfire seedling recruitment at various fire intervals in Banksia woodlands is warranted to confirm minimum tolerable fire intervals and further explore variation along environmental gradients.

Additional evidence is also needed to test the assumptions of the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum intervals, including whether the 2×rule of thumb (Gill and Nicholls 1989) adequately covers natural variation in (1) seed bank accumulation rates and (2) flowering, pollination and seed set for species with different traits. At our estimated minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations had reached 22%–84% of their predicted maximum flowering output, and serotinous species had produced cones over at least 3–4 years and had reached 45%–91% of their predicted maximum canopy seed bank accumulation. Variation in post-fire reproductive attributes among species potentially indicates that the efficacy of the 2×approximation of minimum tolerable fire intervals varies between species. Perhaps species with soil-stored seed banks might be more adequately covered by the 2×approximation than those with canopy seed banks, as species with soil-stored seed may possess a residual seed bank after fire (i.e., seed banks are not completely exhausted by fire) (Auld and Denham 2006) and do not have to produce a persistent woody fruit requiring resources like serotinous species (Cramer and Midgley 2009; Tonnabel et al. 2012\). Our results also demonstrate substantial variation in reproduction owing to varying environmental conditions, suggesting that, in some cases, the 2×approximation may be inadequate to account for delays in reproduction. For example, for *G. tomentosum*, the presence of herbivores and low mean annual rainfall delayed the juvenile period beyond the estimated minimum tolerable fire interval under average growing conditions.

## **4.2   |   Post-Fire Reproduction**

Fire-killed species are generally considered to have longer primary juvenile periods than the secondary juvenile periods of cooccurring resprouters (Gosper, Prober, and Yates 2013; Harvey et al. 2017\), but we observed little difference. Similar juvenile periods for these species groups, however, do not necessarily mean that they have equivalent reproductive trajectories or would be expected to have similar fire interval responses given differences in other traits. For example, resprouters may have a much lower maximum reproductive output at peak maturity compared to co-occurring fire-killed species owing to differences in resource allocation to reproduction versus energy storage (Enright and Lamont 1989\). Also, by the onset of reproductive maturity, resprouters have likely developed a strong resprouting capacity, potentially surviving through several fires before reaching a highly reproductive stage (Enright and Lamont 1992\), although resprouting and reproductive capacity may be eroded by a series of short fire intervals (Enright et al. 2011; Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett 2016). In contrast, fire-killed species may require several years after reaching reproductive maturity to develop adequate reproductive capacity for recovery after subsequent fires and therefore could be at risk of decline at the same intervals at which resprouters can readily resprout. There is an obvious advantage for fire-killed species in fire-prone habitats to reach maximum reproductive capacity as quickly as possible, and probably soon after the onset of reproduction, as indicated by our juvenile period data.

For the fire-killed species with the longest juvenile period studied here (*B. prionotes*), some plants produced cones following the first year of flowering (4 years post-fire), and the corresponding estimated minimum tolerable fire interval (8years) allowed populations to reach, on average, 56% of their maximum flower production and 91% of their maximum canopy seed bank size. For a related, fire-killed *Banksia* species, Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [\(1996) similarly showed that plants began producing cones after the first year of flowering and produced an increasing number of cones in the following few years. Despite being the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species in this study, and probably in Banksia woodlands generally, *B. prionotes* appears to have a relatively short juvenile period compared to other fire-killed species in southwestern Australia (Gosper et al. 2022; Harvey et al. 2017; Wooller, Wooller, and Brown 2002\). Populations of *B. prionotes* also often occur in discrete stands such that a conservative minimum interval of 10 years, under average growing conditions, may not necessarily be relevant to apply to the entire landscape, or where fires are sufficiently patchy or of low severity to allow established individuals to survive fire (Burrows and Middleton 2016). Intervals less than 10years are relatively rare on the Swan Coastal Plain, especially in areas with managed fire regimes, although changing climate regimes and increasing human disturbance do not necessarily preclude such intervals (Fontaine 2022\).

{15}

=== PAGE 17 ===


Our findings are consistent with previous efforts from the region in quantifying post-fire seed production in the resprouting *B. attenuata* in showing that mature trees are capable of producing cones in the first year or two after fire because they can resprout epicormically (Densmore and Clingan 2019; Valentine et al. 2014). Post-fire cone production is mediated by fire severity, where there are minimal interruptions to reproduction after low severity fire, but trees may take several years to regain the same level of cone production after high severity fire (Densmore and Clingan 2019). By the time of the species-specific minimum tolerable fire interval estimated here (~9 years), Valentine et al. [\(2014) estimated that mature adults (>2m tall) had accumulated, on average, approximately 6 cones per plant, which is higher than estimates presented here (~1 cone per plant). Our dataset includes smaller juvenile plants and a subset of our data on *B. attenuata* trees >2m tall shows cone counts across a similar range of values to Valentine et al. [\(2014\). Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016) and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019) report around 1.3 and 7 times higher estimates of *B. attenuata* mean canopy seed bank density (cones per ha), respectively, than we find here (mean 746 cones per ha; Figure [S3\). However, Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016\) included higher rainfall sites on the Swan Coastal Plain and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019) reported on the entire crop of cones for ease of recording regardless of whether they had closed follicles or not, where, in both cases, it would be reasonable to expect higher canopy seed bank estimates. Interestingly, the much higher estimates of cones per ha reported by Densmore and Clingan [\(2019\) can be explained by the weakly serotinous nature of *B. attenuata* in the region (Cowling and Lamont 1985), where most seeds are released from cones within two years of seed maturity, but opened cones are likely retained on the plant for many years, and could therefore give the impression of a much larger canopy seed bank. Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016) reported a similar trend of gradually increasing seed bank size with increasing time since fire for *B. attenuata* and a similar range of values for cones per ha for *B. prionotes*.

We show that plants of fire-killed shrubs that regenerate via seed following fire gain reproductive capacity quickly. Likewise, Monk, Pate, and Loneragan [\(1981) observed that the fire-killed *A. pulchella* began producing flowers and seeds in the second year after fire, and achieved maximum seed production shortly thereafter (3–4 years post-fire). These observations differ from those for fire-killed Proteaceae shrubs from southeastern Australia where cone and seed production was not observed for a few years after first flowering, and was slower overall (Jenkins, Morrison, and Auld 2010). For fast-growing species such as *A. pulchella*, a doubling of the juvenile period as a general rule of thumb for estimating the minimum tolerable fire interval may be adequate to sustain populations under average growing conditions, even if this only allows for one or two additional years of seed production. Rapid post-fire reproductive maturity and abundant seed production are important mechanisms to cope with short fire intervals for species adapted to frequent canopy scorch, whether that be understorey shrubs scorched in all but the lowest severity fires, or trees burnt in crown fire regimes (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula 1996; Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon 1996\). Likewise, soil-stored seed banks, variable seed dormancy and residual seedbanks are traits that allow species to cope with short fire intervals. Banksia woodlands may be adapted to mixed severity fire regimes where understorey and overstorey components experience a range of low, moderate and high severity fire at widely varying intervals, potentially as short as 5–10 years in the understorey (Hobbs and Atkins 1990; Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024\).

Our findings for the resprouting shrub *A. humilis* are consistent with expectations for dioecious species in that patterns of postfire flowering appear to be driven by the costs of male versus female reproduction (Barrett and Hough 2012; Obeso 2002\). Flower and pollen production in male plants is less costly than flower, cone and seed production in female plants and so we would expect to observe precocious male flowering (Field, Pickup, and Barrett 2013). In comparison to female plants, male *A. humilis* plants had a shorter juvenile period (2.5 vs. 3.5years on average), produced more flowers per plant on average across all fire ages (927 vs. 269) and produced more flowers on average at any given plant size.

Wilson et al. [\(2014\) provided an estimate of 40 years for the maximum tolerable fire interval for Banksia woodlands based on the maximum longevity of serotinous, fire-killed *Banksia* species. However, *Banksia* longevity was derived for a different species (*B. hookeriana*) from a nearby region with different climate and fire regimes, and for a species that grows as a tall shrub rather than a tree, and therefore presumably has a shorter lifespan (Cowling and Lamont 1985\). We expect *Banksia* tree longevity in the range of 40–60 years for *B. prionotes* (fire-killed) and to exceed 100 years for *B. attenuata* (resprouter). Over the approximately 35-year chronosequence studied here, we found no evidence of decline in reproduction for *B. attenuata*, but some evidence for a minor decline in reproduction in *B. prionotes* which appears primarily driven by a decline in plant density of mature stages with a minor contribution from a decline in reproductive output per plant. Although *B. prionotes* can have low levels of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024\), this input of non-reproductive individuals does not appear to have a noticeable effect on population-level reproduction (Figure [S5\). There is little evidence of major population senescence in *B. prionotes*, and therefore, maximum tolerable intervals are likely to exceed 40years, which are very rare regardless (Wilson et al. 2014).

#### **4.3   |   Reproduction Under Varying Environmental and Demographic Conditions**

Environmental productivity (mean annual rainfall) and the presence or absence of herbivory were found to be important factors associated with post-fire reproductive trajectories (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward 2008; Gosper et al. 2022; McCaw 2008\). In sites with low mean rainfall (low productivity) or herbivore presence, predicted juvenile periods were delayed by up to 3 years, and therefore minimum tolerable fire intervals by up to 6 years for fire-killed understorey shrubs (*A. pulchella* and *G. tomentosum*). Low mean rainfall also decreased flower production by up to 61% for the same species. For short-lived species, this may represent a doubling (or more) of the minimum fire-free period required for population replacement, and potentially a reduction in lifetime reproductive output.

{16}

=== PAGE 18 ===


While these data pertain to mean rainfall and the prevailing presence or absence of herbivores, our results suggest that delayed reproductive maturity and reduced reproductive output could occur under abrupt environmental changes such as the introduction of native or non-native herbivores, or the increasing severity of drought conditions associated with climate change (Gosper et al. 2022; Matusick et al. 2018\). Modelling suggests that primary juvenile periods for serotinous obligate seeders (here represented by *B. prionotes*) could more than double in the study area under 2050 climate change scenarios, including lower mean annual rainfall (Gosper et al. 2022\), potentially requiring longer fire intervals to conserve vulnerable populations. In general, we sampled across a relatively narrow mean annual rainfall gradient (~150mm difference) compared to the variation present in the broader region, and in particular, our sampling of *B. prionotes* populations occurred across a very narrow range (30mm difference). It is not surprising, therefore, that we did not detect an effect of rainfall for *B. prionotes*; however, if sampling was repeated across a wider rainfall gradient (spatial or temporal), we would expect to detect slower maturity rates under low rainfall. This is a broad concern for fire-killed species which rely on post-fire recruitment from seeds for persistence, and is consistent with the concept of 'interval squeeze' where populations are vulnerable to decline with the simultaneous shortening of fire intervals and reduced seed production and post-fire recruitment associated with climate change impacts (Enright et al. 2015\). Invasive grassy weeds are also a significant threat in Banksia woodlands (Ritchie et al. 2021\), and may pose an additional limitation on population recovery if weeds reduce post-fire seedling recruitment or delay maturation and reproductive maturity.

The effects of varying mean annual rainfall on flowering rate (juvenile period) provided a curious result for *B. attenuata*, where populations in high mean rainfall sites appeared to mature more slowly than populations in low mean rainfall sites. Rather than higher rainfall delaying maturation, we believe this relates to differences in the demographic structure of populations under varying rainfall regimes altering population-level calculations. In the study area, higher rainfall and longer growing seasons likely facilitate higher rates of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024\), although not to a level that would result in densification or canopy closure that would, in turn, preclude recruitment of shade-intolerant seedlings and probably reduce reproductive output. Flowering rates reported here are a composite of reproduction (or lack thereof) in seedlings, juveniles and adults, and therefore a higher proportion of non-reproductive seedlings and juveniles resulting from higher recruitment will lower flowering rate estimates.

Canopy seed banks (closed cone counts per plant) for both *Banksia* species were very low, with *B. attenuata* generally having less than two seed-bearing cones per plant on average, and *B. prionotes* generally less than one. Low cone counts can be explained by a combination of the weakly serotinous nature of these *Banksia* species in the study area, and demographic structures with a high proportion of juvenile plants with little to no reproduction (Figures [S5 and [S6). Cowling and Lamont [\(1985) reported a gradient in the degree of serotiny of *Banksia* species in the region with populations in our study area being weakly or non-serotinous, meaning that the majority of the accumulated canopy seed bank originates from the most recent seed crop minus any losses from

disease and predation. Whelan and Ayre [\(2020\) likewise reported very low canopy seed bank accumulation for a serotinous *Banksia* shrub species from southeastern Australia. Both weakly serotinous *Banksia* species studied here develop multi-cohort populations, especially in the absence of fire (Hobbs and Atkins 1990; Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024). Like the effect of rainfall on *B. attenuata* flowering rate noted above, a high proportion of non-reproductive juvenile plants lowers population-level seed bank size estimates which likely underestimates the reproductive potential of mature individuals. While mature individuals have the potential to contribute much larger seed banks, weak serotiny will ultimately limit the maximum size of the canopy seed bank. This contrasts with the seed bank dynamics of highly serotinous *Banksia* species in ecosystems with more regular crown fire regimes where canopy seed banks can accumulate over many years (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula 1996\).

Top-ranked models explained up to 92% of variation in the data (mean=43%, inter-quartile range=30%–51%; Table [2, Table [5\), leaving, in some cases, substantial variation unexplained by the variables considered in this study. More detailed analyses of the effects of interannual weather variation and spatially varying site variables (e.g., soil type, aspect, elevation) could explain greater variation in the data and provide a deeper understanding of the drivers of reproduction. The analysis presented here using mean annual rainfall could also be extended to quantify the effects of varying rainfall at different demographic stages—for example, during seedling establishment (1–2years post-fire), floral initiation and fruit development—to assess the sensitivity of post-fire reproduction to extreme dry climate conditions. Such analyses could help predict scenarios or sites under which fire managers may need to consider longer managed fire intervals to accommodate delayed juvenile periods under increasingly common droughts and heatwave events (Matusick et al. 2018; Ruthrof et al. 2021\).

#### **4.4   |   Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction**

While we found that TSF was a clear indicator of reproduction, we also show that plant size is a much stronger predictor of reproductive capacity as also reported elsewhere by Andrus et al. [\(2020\), Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [\(1993) and von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [\(2018\). Many plant species that inhabit fire-prone environments (especially fire-killed species in stand-replacing fire regimes) are often assumed to follow a specific post-fire trajectory where a single, post-fire seedling cohort matures and grows larger at a similar rate (Gill and McMahon 1986). However, this assumption may weaken in noncrown fire regimes, or for multi-cohort populations resulting from inter-fire recruitment, post-fire resprouting, or both. Interfire recruitment is evident for most of the species studied here (Hobbs and Atkins 1990; Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. 2024\), and therefore, population-level metrics of reproduction may be more closely related to varying demographic structure or environmental conditions rather than TSF.

We acknowledge TSF and post-fire juvenile periods as simplistic yet useful indicators of post-fire reproductive maturity, but here we show that the effects of other environmental and demographic conditions can introduce substantial variation into species 

{17}

=== PAGE 19 ===


responses, and therefore are important to consider when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence (Gosper et al. 2022). As originally recognised, the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals can provide rapid and low-cost guidance for fire management planning, but advances in ecological understanding and technology for measuring vegetation attributes should allow for the development of more sophisticated models for predicting variation in reproduction by including multiple environmental and demographic variables. Other metrics of species reproductive maturity and minimum tolerable fire intervals that may provide useful alternative or supplemental information for fire managers include the assessment of (1) the reproductive output (and density) of the largest individuals as the plants that contribute most to the reproductive capacity of the population and (2) average understorey plant height and litter cover as surrogates of plant growth and fuel accumulation. Ongoing advances in the mapping of vegetation structure from remote sensing data (e.g., through airborne or terrestrial laser scanning) (Moudrý et al. 2023; Turner et al. 2023) may provide an opportunity to measure plant size and density across large areas and combine with environmental and demographic data, such as that presented in this study, to calculate metrics of reproduction at a similar landscape scale to traditional fire age mapping currently used extensively in fire management planning.

*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518

# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**

R. A. BRADSTOCK\*

*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*

M. A. O'CONNELL

*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*

#### **Abstract**

*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*

*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*

*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*

#### **Introduction**

Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).

The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).

Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-

\*Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.




=== PAGE 2 ===


506 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).

These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.

(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?

(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?

(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?

(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?

(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?

#### **Methods**

#### *Study sites*

The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.

Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.

#### *Seedling emergence and survival*

The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m<sup>2</sup>) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.

The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.




=== PAGE 3 ===


*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 507

Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.

#### *Survival in established plants*

Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.

Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.

Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.

Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.

#### *Seed-survival*

Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.

Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.

Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.

The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.




=== PAGE 4 ===


508 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

#### *Seed-bank estimation*

All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and nonlinear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.

Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.

A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.

#### *Seed-release between fires*

The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.

All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.

#### *The effect of frequent fires*

The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.

Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:

*N* = *B* × *E* × *Ss* × *Se* (1)

where *B* = first generation seed-bank size, *E* = proportion of seeds emerging as post-fire seedlings, *Ss* = proportion of seedlings which survive and *Se* = proportion of living plants > 3 years old at *i* years of age. Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.

#### **Results**

#### *Seedling emergence and survival*

In both species, emergence was spread over periods of up to 9 months after the fires or experiments. The number, density and proportion of seedlings that emerged from seeds were variable (Table 1). Pulses of emergence pro-

The alternative values of E were set at 0.5 and 0.05. These bounded the range observed in the field (Table 1). #### **Discussion**

#### *Effects of frequent fires*

The importance of emergence and survival was reffected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk of a decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1,2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.

Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.

Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation.

Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.

While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (< 100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.

After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau of Meterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in post-fire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.

4	*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518
5	
6	# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**
7	
8	R. A. BRADSTOCK\*
9	
10	*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*
11	
12	M. A. O'CONNELL
13	
14	*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*
15	
16	#### **Abstract**
17	
18	*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*
19	
20	*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*
21	
22	*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*
23	
24	#### **Introduction**
25	
26	Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).
27	
28	The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).
29	
30	Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-
31	
32	\*Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.
33	
34	
35	
36	
37	=== PAGE 2 ===
38	
39	
40	506 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
41	
42	ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).
43	
44	These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.
45	
46	(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?
47	
48	(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?
49	
50	(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?
51	
52	(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?
53	
54	(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?
55	
56	#### **Methods**
57	
58	#### *Study sites*
59	
60	The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.
61	
62	Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.
63	
64	#### *Seedling emergence and survival*
65	
66	The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m<sup>2</sup>) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.
67	
68	The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.
69	
70	
71	
72	
73	=== PAGE 3 ===
74	
75	
76	*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 507
77	
78	Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.
79	
80	#### *Survival in established plants*
81	
82	Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.
83	
84	Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.
85	
86	Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.
87	
88	Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.
89	
90	#### *Seed-survival*
91	
92	Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.
93	
94	Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.
95	
96	Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.
97	
98	The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.
99	
100	
101	
102	
103	=== PAGE 4 ===
104	
105	
106	508 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*
107	
108	#### *Seed-bank estimation*
109	
110	All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and nonlinear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.
111	
112	Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.
113	
114	A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.
115	
116	#### *Seed-release between fires*
117	
118	The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.
119	
120	All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.
121	
122	#### *The effect of frequent fires*
123	
124	The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.
125	
126	Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:
127

Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.

More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years.
